Q: Race condition on large systems A:

Critical sections or mutexes are limited to intra-process threads, so to manage concurrent threads across multiple processes (like the multiple app instances or multiple databases you mention), you would need some kind of centralized lock service.

Open-source examples of lock services include:

  • Apache ZooKeeper
  • HashiCorp Consul
  • Redis or Valkey
  • Etcd

Some RDBMS products also include user-level lock commands, such as GET_LOCK() in MySQL or pg_advisory_lock() in PostgreSQL. The system may have multiple database instances, so the apps would all need to designate a single database instance that manages these locks.

Another strategy is to use a message queue service. For example, after the first process commits its transaction, it pushes a message into the queue. Dependent processes wait for that message to appear in the queue.

What all these methods have in common is that they cooperate in using a central service that all the apps have access to. This allows the locking to work outside the scope of a single process.

Q: Speeding up the load time of a Java Applet in a browser control A:

You can profile the java applet and the networking, the stall can be anywhere.

You can try having a hot jvm, but due to jvm warm up, I do not expect it to be better than just letting it load normally.

Q: How can I install from a git subdirectory with pip? A:

The latest docs discourage the use of the #egg=pkg URL fragment. Instead, they suggest to use only the subdirectory fragment:

For example, if your package pkg is in subdirectory pkg_dir:

python -m pip install "pkg @ git+https://git@github.com/org/repo.git#subdirectory=pkg_dir"

Note that pkg @ seems optional, at least for pyproject.toml projects.

Q: ip link set command throws error.RTNETLINK answers: Operation not permitted A:

You made a tun device but you're trying to give it a MAC. That won't work, and it isn't really a permissions problem even though the error says so.

A tun is a layer 3 interface. It carries bare IP packets, there's no Ethernet header, so it has no hardware address at all. ip link set ... address has nothing to set on it and the driver rejects the call. On my machine the exact wording is "Operation not supported" rather than "not permitted", but it's the same cause. The errno the tun driver hands back for a set-mac has moved around between kernel versions.

You can see there's nothing to set:

ip -d link show tun0

A tun shows link/none and the NOARP flag. A normal ethernet-style device shows link/ether with an address next to it.

You called it a "virtual Ethernet device", so what you actually want is a tap, not a tun. A tap is layer 2 (real Ethernet frames), and it has a MAC you can set:

sudo ip tuntap add dev tap0 mode tap sudo ip link set dev tap0 address 54:e1:ad:b9:12:ee sudo ip addr add 192.168.82.22/24 dev tap0 sudo ip link set dev tap0 up

If you really did mean tun (layer 3, say a VPN endpoint), then just drop the ip link set address line. A tun doesn't need a MAC and can't take one, the ip addr add you already ran is all it wants.

Q: How can I locate an element in a nested div without selecting the outer div? A:

The outer div matches because has: looks at descendants at any depth, and the heading is a descendant of both divs. Three ways to fix it:

1. Use a direct-child CSS :has() — only matches the div whose immediate child is the heading:

await page
  .locator('div:has(> h1:text-is("first item"))')
  .getByRole('button', { name: 'buy now' })
  .click();

2. Start from the heading and go up to its parent:

await page
  .getByRole('heading', { name: 'first item' })
  .locator('..')
  .getByRole('button', { name: 'buy now' })
  .click();

3. Keep your filter, but first exclude divs that contain other divs:

await page
  .locator('div')
  .filter({ hasNot: page.locator('div') })
  .filter({ has: page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'first item' }) })
  .getByRole('button', { name: 'buy now' })
  .click();

Q: What is the maximum number of threads a process can have in windows A:

The actual limit is determined by the amount of available memory in various ways.

There is no limit of "you can't have more than this many" threads or processes in Windows. There is, however, a limit to how much memory you can use within the system. When that memory runs out, you can't create more threads.

See this MicroSoft Learn blog - Pushing the Limits of Windows: Processes and Threads for more details
